lessons.title: Cement and Capital Goods: Capacity Utilisation, Order Books, and Execution

body.text: Cement and capital goods both sell into India's construction boom, but they are opposite businesses. Cement is a regional commodity where the price of a bag this month decides the quarter. Capital goods and engineering firms lock in years of revenue through orders, then live or die on whether they execute those orders profitably and get paid.

children.text: UltraTech Cement, Ambuja Cements, ACC, Shree Cement, Dalmia Bharat, and JK Cement on one side. Larsen & Toubro, Siemens, ABB India, Thermax, Cummins India, BHEL, KEC International, and Kalpataru Projects on the other. Both groups are bets on India building things, and both are highly cyclical, but the numbers you track are completely different.
Cement: A National Industry With Regional Prices

markDefs.definition: The average distance cement travels from a plant to the customer. Because freight is a large part of cement cost, a shorter lead distance means a lower cost per tonne and better margins.

children.text: Cement is heavy, cheap per tonne, and expensive to transport, so it cannot travel far before freight eats the margin. That single fact shapes the whole industry. Companies compete regionally, not nationally, and prices in the north, south, east, west, and central markets can move independently. A key metric is
. Plants also need limestone, so they are built near limestone reserves, and split grinding units are set up closer to customers to cut freight.

Demand comes mainly from housing, with individual home builders a large chunk, followed by infrastructure projects and commercial construction. That makes cement volumes a good real-time read on both rural housing and government capex. Cement is also seasonal: construction slows during the monsoon and peaks in the January to March quarter as builders rush to finish before the financial year ends.

body.title: Illustrative Seasonality of Cement Volumes (Index, Average Quarter = 100)

body.text: Because of this seasonality, never compare a cement company's July to September quarter with the previous January to March quarter and conclude the business is deteriorating. Compare each quarter with the same quarter a year earlier, and watch region-wise price and volume commentary.

body.title: What a ₹20 Price Hike Is Worth
body.prompt: The illustrative cement company above sells 25 million tonnes a year. Prices rise by ₹20 per 50 kg bag and costs stay unchanged. By how much does its annual EBITDA increase, in ₹ crore?
body.explanation: ₹20 per bag × 20 bags = ₹400 per tonne. On 25 million tonnes, that is ₹400 × 2.5 crore tonnes = ₹1,000 crore. EBITDA per tonne rises from ₹900 to ₹1,300, a 44% jump in operating profit from a price increase of about 8% per bag. This is why cement analysts track weekly regional price data so closely.

body.title: Utilisation, consolidation, and why cement prices behave the way they do

children.text: Cement has heavy fixed costs, so a plant running below capacity carries a high fixed cost per tonne, as you calculated in Chapter 2. When an industry or a region has far more capacity than demand, producers compete on price to fill kilns, and margins collapse. When utilisation climbs toward 80% and above, producers gain confidence to raise prices. This is why utilisation is the single best predictor of cement pricing power, and why investors watch industry capacity additions as closely as demand.

Indian cement has also been consolidating, with large acquisitions since 2022 concentrating capacity among fewer big groups. Consolidation can support pricing discipline in a region, but it can also trigger market share battles when a large player pushes for volume. Read management commentary on whether the company is prioritising price or volume; the two rarely improve together.
Capital Goods: The Order Book Business

Engineering, construction, and capital goods companies win contracts today and convert them into revenue over the following years. So their disclosures revolve around three numbers: order inflow, the value of new orders won in the quarter; order book, the total value of orders won but not yet executed; and revenue, the portion recognised as work is completed. Dividing the order book by trailing annual revenue gives book-to-bill, roughly how many years of work is already in hand.

body.caption: How many years of revenue the company has already contracted

body.title: Calculate Book-to-Bill
body.prompt: An engineering and construction company reports an order book of ₹4,50,000 crore and revenue of ₹2,25,000 crore over the last twelve months. What is its book-to-bill ratio, in years? Round to one decimal place.
body.explanation: ₹4,50,000 crore ÷ ₹2,25,000 crore = 2.0 years of revenue already contracted. A rising book-to-bill means visibility is improving; a falling one means execution is outpacing new wins, which eventually slows revenue growth. Always check both the ratio and the trend in quarterly order inflow.

columns.label: Product companies (for example Siemens, ABB India, Cummins India)
points: Sell equipment such as motors, switchgear, transformers, and engines
Shorter order cycles and more standardised products
Typically higher margins and lighter working capital
Often trade at premium valuations for consistency

columns.label: Project companies (for example L&T, KEC International, Kalpataru Projects)
points: Execute large multi-year construction and engineering contracts
Revenue recognised as work progresses, over years
Thinner margins and heavy working capital in receivables and retention money
Exposed to cost overruns, delays, and client payment cycles

body.text: A record order book is not a record profit. Orders can be won at thin margins to keep plants and teams busy, fixed-price contracts can be hit by commodity inflation, execution can be delayed by land or clearance issues, and government clients can pay slowly. Judge an order book by its profitability and cash conversion, not just its size.

body.title: Record Order Book, Missing Cash
body.scenario: An infrastructure EPC company reports its highest ever order book, up 35% year on year, and revenue growth of 20%. But its receivables have grown 55%, unbilled revenue has risen sharply, operating cash flow is negative for the second year running, and short-term borrowings are up. Around 70% of the order book is from state government agencies. EBITDA margin has slipped by 120 basis points because of higher input costs on fixed-price contracts.
body.prompt: What is your assessment, and what would you want to see before trusting the order book?
body.modelAnswer: The order book is growing faster than the company can convert it into cash, which is the classic warning sign in project businesses. Receivables growing much faster than revenue, rising unbilled revenue, and two years of negative operating cash flow together suggest the company is funding its clients' projects with borrowed money. Heavy exposure to state government agencies raises the risk of slow payments and disputed claims. Falling margins on fixed-price contracts show it is absorbing commodity inflation rather than passing it on. Before trusting the order book, look for: the ageing of receivables and how much is overdue beyond a year; how unbilled revenue is converting into bills; working capital days trending down; the share of orders with price escalation clauses; the mix of private and central government clients; management guidance on execution timelines; and interest costs as a share of EBITDA, since debt-funded working capital eats into profits. A smaller order book with clean cash conversion is worth more than a record one that never turns into money.

body.title: Which Order Book Is Highest Quality?
body.question: Four engineering companies have order books of similar size. Which one is most likely to translate into profitable, cash-generating revenue?
options: Orders mostly from one state agency, fixed price, with long payment cycles
A diversified mix of private sector and central government orders, many with price escalation clauses, and working capital days trending down
A single very large order won at aggressive pricing to enter a new geography
Orders with long execution timelines and heavy exposure to imported components priced in dollars, unhedged
body.explanation: Diversified clients reduce concentration risk, price escalation clauses protect margins against commodity inflation, and improving working capital shows orders are converting into cash. The other options concentrate payment risk, sacrifice margin for entry, or leave the company exposed to input cost and currency swings.

body.title: Fill in the Blank
body.textWithBlank: Dividing an engineering company's order book by its trailing twelve month revenue gives the ___ ratio, which shows how many years of work it has in hand.
body.explanation: Book-to-bill measures revenue visibility. A rising ratio means order wins are outpacing execution.

body.title: Tracking Cement and Capital Goods Companies
steps: For cement, track EBITDA per tonne, realisation per tonne, and cost per tonne over the last eight quarters
Check regional price trends and the company's exposure by region, since pricing is regional
Check capacity utilisation for the company and the industry, and note announced capacity additions
Compare quarters year on year rather than sequentially, because of monsoon seasonality
For capital goods, track quarterly order inflow, order book, book-to-bill, and execution commentary
Test order book quality: client mix, fixed price versus escalation clauses, and geography
Check working capital days, receivables ageing, unbilled revenue, and operating cash flow against reported profit

points: Cement is a regional business because freight is expensive, so lead distance and regional prices drive profitability
EBITDA per tonne is the core cement metric, and small price changes per bag move profits sharply
Capacity utilisation predicts cement pricing power, and cement volumes are seasonal, weak in the monsoon and strongest in January to March
Capital goods and engineering companies are judged on order inflow, order book, and book-to-bill, which measures years of contracted revenue
Product companies have higher margins and lighter working capital than project companies executing multi-year contracts
A record order book means little without profitable pricing and cash conversion; watch receivables, unbilled revenue, and operating cash flow
